                            The graph of the function $g(h)$ is shown above, where

$$
g(h)=\frac{4}{h}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-1).
$$

From the graph, what is ${lim}_{h\to \,0}g(h)?$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

feedback.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's sketch the graph of $y=f(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14262363/assets/446f0fd704e09106f34a70fcbd3adb2806bfea13664114bd5d704fd3c8519001.png)

As $x$ decreases to $-\infty $, the graph oscillates between the values $y=-4$ and $y=4$ indefinitely. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=DNE.
$$

We have the function $f(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).$ Notice that we are given the length $h$ of the interval. So, the average rate of change of $f$ over this interval is given by

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

with $a=0.$ Substituting into the formula and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \\  & =\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{0}{2})}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4(1)}{h} \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-4}{h} \\  & =\frac{4}{h}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{h}{2})-1).\end{aligned}
$$
